speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege relating to an answer given yesterday to question No. 431 as found on page 1810 of Hansard. This answer is wrong. The first part of the answer states that a site consisting of two parcels of land for a public building at Britt, Ontario, is being acquired by the government from G. M. Taylor. The second part of the answer states that Mr. Taylor is not a consultant of the Minister of Public Works or of the Postmaster General.
This latter answer is in error, because I asked a question on December 4, 1963, which is to be found on page 5409 of Hansard, relating to the consultants of the Postmaster General. The third part of that question was as follows:
From whom were recommendations for this appointment solicited by the Postmaster General?
This was the answer:
District director of postal service. North Bay, and Gerald M. Taylor.
This gentleman is a twice defeated Liberal candidate. My reason for raising a question of privilege with regard to the question answered yesterday is to indicate that he has used his position and knowledge to go out and take an option on a public site required by the government and then resell the property to the government. I am directing this matter to the attention of the minister and I would ask him to look into it, correct the answer and possibly also get a new consultant.

Mr. Speaker, under standing order 26 I should like to ask leave to adjourn the business of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, the extension of the winter works program past April 30, in the areas adversely affected by a more severe climate.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the motion is quite in order and ought to be accepted by all members of this house.
It deals with a very specific question: the extension of winter works, after April 30, in areas where the climate is more severe. The matter is one of public importance. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) himself stated recently that unemployment was the number one problem facing the government today. Now, unemployment is especially high in areas which have to put up with a severe climate. At the present time it represents Canada's most acute problem.
It is obviously a matter of general interest, since it concerns a large number of regions, in all parts of the country, especially Newfoundland, New Brunswick, the province of Quebec, northern Ontario, a large part of Saskatchewan, northern Manitoba and northern Alberta.

I have to decide whether the ordinary proceedings before the house should be adjourned under standing order 26, and to determine whether the motion moved by the hon. member for Lapointe is in order. The three essentials, of course, are that the question must be national in scope, there must be extreme urgency, and there must be lack of other opportunity to debate the matter.

It seems to me that with certain estimates under discussion later this day and with the budget debate just around the corner, so to speak, there will be ample opportunity before April 30 to discuss this interesting matter. speechtext:
A week ago-I think it was the last day on which the hon. gentleman was here- he asked me a question with regard to the disbandment of R.C.A.F. No. 410 all-weather fighter squadron at R.C.A.F. station Uplands. This action was the outcome of the consolidation of air defence squadrons announced January 10. Previously the relatively small number of Voodoo aircraft belonging to the R.C.A.F.'s air defence command had been dispersed through five squadrons in five different locations. Although they were called "squadrons" they had a unit establishment of only 12 aircraft each, and this was long considered to be an expensive and not too efficient way of operating such a small force. Such an arrangement inevitably means a great deal of administrative, technical and support overhead for the amount of fighting effectiveness produced.
After studying the cost-effectiveness of this arrangement, I accepted the R.C.A.F. recommendation that the Voodoo aircraft could be more effective grouped in three squadrons


rather than five. No. 410 squadron was selected by the R.C.A.F. as one of the two squadrons to be placed on the inactive list. The other would be No. 414 squadron located at North Bay, effective July 1 this year.
I am sure hon. members will join me in thanking the fine officers, N.C.O.'s and men of this proud squadron for the outstanding service they have given to our country.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED ADOPTION BY CANADA OF FREE

speechtext: have a question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. According to a news report in this morning's Globe and Mail, Under Secretary of State Norman Robertson, who leads a Canadian negotiating team to trade talks in Geneva in May, is likely to have a strong free trade mandate from Canadian business. Is this an indication that the government has adopted a free trade policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORTED ADOPTION BY CANADA OF FREE
subtopic: TRADE POLICY
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman asked this question, because it gives me an opportunity of reporting in a brief way on what has been going on in this field.
First of all, in reply to the particular question which he raised arising out of the report in the Globe and Mail, I may say this report was apparently written as a result of repeated questioning by representatives of the press of the acting chairman, Mr. Hector McKinnon. He, in reply to these questions, had emphatically and frequently stated that since all submissions to the committee are regarded as confidential, no specific information could be supplied regarding the representations made by any industry or any industries.
In reply to frequent further inquiries as to whether the general trend of the submissions was in the direction of no reductions on Canadian tariffs, the committee has answered in general terms as follows. First, Canadian industry, contemplating the Kennedy round, appears today to be seized of the possibilities and potentialities in export trade and is providing to the committee many specific requests regarding concessions desired in the tariffs of other countries. Second, in many instances submissions state that provided the concessions requested are forthcoming, the applicant industry or company would be prepared to forgo at least part of the protection afforded by the Canadian tariff. On the whole the submissions reaching the committee are helpful and constructive, but by

no means could it be said that, again on the whole, they favour or suggest the adoption of a policy of free trade.

maintopic: REPORTED ADOPTION BY CANADA OF FREE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these negotiations will proceed over a very long period of time. Mr. Chairman, last night prior to the adjournment of the house, I directed a few questions to the Minister of Justice in order to clarify a situation which, I think, is detrimental to my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order to be in a position to give the hon. member an answer this afternoon, I had a talk with the officials of my department and I obtained certain information. As I expected and mentioned yesterday, I felt sure that we could dismiss political considerations as motives for the decision taken.
I know, for instance, having checked on it myself, that in the case of the Drumheller penitentiary located in the riding of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), the decision was reached by the previous government. While my immediate predecessor was pressed by certain societies and organizations to have the penitentiary built somewhere else than in Drumheller, he had taken the necessary steps to maintain the decision taken and in the same way, the reasons behind the decision concerning the penitentiary originally projected for St. Pie de Bagot, were serious.
It is clear that the decision taken by the government to build a penitentiary in Drumheller was far from being based on political arguments and, particularly on Liberal political reasons.
May I say, for the information of the house, that the construction of that penitentiary might have been delayed if there had been political decisions, but this construction will start in April 1964 and will be completed by March 1966.
In the same way I knew that the decision taken by the previous government to build
[Mr. Hellyer.l
a detention unit in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, a decision by which my immediate predecessor, Hon. Mr. Chevrier, abided, was not maintained because of partisan political reasons. That decision of the previous government was maintained for serious consideration. Construction of the institution will start in June 1964 and will be completed in March 1965.
In view of those facts I was convinced that serious motives must also have determined the decision of my immediate predecessor not to proceed immediately with the construction of a medium security penitentiary at St. Pie de Bagot. Following a decision of the previous administration, two pieces of land were purchased. Since both were to be used for the establishment of two similar institutions, one in St. Pie de Bagot and the other in Cowans-ville, I must inform the house that construction at Cowansville of the medium security penitentiary proposed by the former government was undertaken in November 1963 and will be completed in January 1965.
Since it is the former administration that purchased two plots of land in the province of Quebec, there can be no question of political partisanship, in the case of Cowansville. As for St. Pie de Bagot, we reconsidered the decision merely because of the serious incidents which took place on June 17, 1962, in the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, which is a maximum security institution. It then became evident to this government that an addition to this penitentiary, or if you prefer an additional maximum security detention unit had become necessary, and this is more urgent than building a medium security detention unit.
For those reasons, my predecessor examined the circumstances and factors which had to be considered in that case; he consulted his advisors and asked them whether or not a medium security institution would be useful to supplement the staff or the available facilities at St. Vincent de Paul. Naturally, the answer was no.
Then the question arose as to whether another maximum security penitentiary should not be built instead of that medium security institution. It became clear, on examining the relevant circumstances and factors, that such a thing would be extremely dangerous, because of the relationship which would necessarily exist between the St. Vincent de Paul complex and that additional complex. Well, to establish a system in the public interest, this additional complex would have to be situated, not on the south but on the north shore of the St. Lawrence and this sufficiently near St. Vincent de Paul to avoid any possible danger in the regular transportation of prisoners at least from an institution

Supply-Justice
to another, or from the institution to the courthouse or elsewhere in the institution.
It is clear that as far as convicts which have been given comparatively stiffer penalties are concerned, if the institution were situated on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, it would be a constant threat during transportation, because it is obvious that it would be a frequent and I would even say a constant invitation to underworld characters, to try to escape, or to facilitate the escape of prisoners and to stop cars at any time.
It is obvious that the longer the route followed by vehicles and the more frequent the trips, that is, every day, I believe, the greater the risks I have just mentioned.
But I should like to assure the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot and emphasize that the site at St. Pie de Bagot was not subject to a contract annulment and has not been discarded. This site is and will be preserved until it is necessary to build a medium security institution in the province of Quebec.
In the circumstances I am satisfied that the decision made to change the plans in the case of St. Pie de Bagot was no more political than the one made to proceed with the plans of the previous government in Brome-Missisquoi, Bow River and Prince Albert.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the Minister of Justice for his information, but I think that he lacks some and I am going to prove, beyond the shadow of a doubt that the decision not to go ahead with the construction of St. Pie de Bagot penitentiary is a matter of petty politics on the part of the minister's predecessor. I am sorry to have to speak this way but the reaction from the people in my riding and the documents I have before me force me to do so and to show the house that we are confronted with patronage activities-I have no hesitation in saying it again.
May I go back a little over the background of that matter. On September 18, 1961, as I said yesterday, Hon. Davie Fulton announced the construction of a middle security prison at a cost of $4.5 million in the St. Hyacinthe-Bagot riding.
Of course many problems had to be settled before work could begin. However, Mr. Chairman, as I give you various details you will see for yourself that the Minister of Justice lacks a lot of information which I will be happy to give him.
I have here a contract signed on November 30, 1962, under which the Department of Public Works purchased four properties in the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I also have here a letter addressed to the architect, S. A. Cyr, which reads as follows:

Dear Mr. Cyr:
I wish to confirm our telephone conversation and the discussions that you held with Mr. Simpson, at which time it was intimated that the originally intended young offenders institution is now in abeyance.
The department requires the services of a consultant to develop sketch plans and to prepare working drawings and specifications for a proposed maximum security camp and I would like to have your formal acknowledgment that you are prepared to undertake this work.
This was accepted by Mr. S. A. Cyr. Then there is another letter I want to place on the record. It is dated March 1, 1963, and reads in part as follows:
The original announcement that was made was, as you recall, to the effect that the institution to be constructed at St. Pie would be designed to accommodate 450 inmates and would require a staff of from 150 to 175 officers. Events since that announcement was made (including the disturbance that occurred at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary in June, 1962) have made it necessary to reconsider the program that was originally planned for this area. Let me say, however, that the reconsideration that has been involved is not designed, in any respect, to decrease the size of the operation that was originally planned. The operation will be at least as large as was originally contemplated and, if any changes are required, they will be designed to increase the size of the operation.
Here we have in black and white the fact that it was the intention of the department to build such an establishment at St. Pie. I know the minister has spoken in good faith. He comes here and stands up and says that the situation is contrary to what I have stated. He speaks in good faith but I say he has not got all the information he should have, and I am glad to supplement the information he needs. In a letter dated January 23, 1963, there is the following:
Construction is to start within three months on the first phase of the project-the construction of facilities to accommodate the more hardened criminals from St. Vincent de Paul institution. Within 15 months construction will start on the main institution along the lines originally proposed.
These are the facts, Mr. Chairman, and I am sorry that the minister did not have all the information he needed to have in order to establish the facts as they are before the committee. There is another letter dated April 10, 1963, from Mr. Cyr which reads in part as follows:
Kindly consider the present as my acceptance of the terms of employment of consulting architects as issued by the Department of Public Works of Canada.
I have here a copy of the terms according to which the architect was supposed to act on this project.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member agree with me that after April 22-not after April 8 last-Hon. Davie Fulton, no more than the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot for whom I have great esteem-could hardly claim to speak on behalf of the government?

I wonder, Mr. Chairman,
whether the minister rose to ask me a question or whether he merely attempted to smother the flame. Yet he should know that it is easily lit up again.
In concluding I may say that last year I tried over and over again to get information on the intentions of the government. 

I always received evasive answers. Yesterday I tried to draw the minister's parliamentary secretary into the discussion. It is peculiar that he was here yesterday but is not here this afternoon, when he could justify the answer he gave. In any case, last year I was completely unable to get any information on the intentions of the government. However, by a fortunate conjunction of circumstances I received a specific answer last Friday. I may thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) for sticking his nose where he should not have, but he told this house that the matter of the St. Pie de Bagot penitentiary was definitely settled, that the problem was definitely disposed of, that there was nothing more contemplated there. And yet, even today, the Minister of Justice says that that land is kept for future use.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to call the attention of the house to the fact that public funds were used for that purpose. A sum of $83,000 was spent to purchase land on which to build a penal institution. Professional people were paid to make studies in that connection. And then everything was cancelled, just to punish the electors of the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot because they had dared to send a Progressive Conservative member to the house.
This is no way to curry favour with citizens of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. The citizens of this constituency are more and more set against the government and they only wait for an opportunity to prove, once more, to those who laughed at the people of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, that they have a long memory and will remember the very undemocratic attitude the Liberal government showed while it was supposed to re-establish on stronger basis the relationship between the citizens of the country.
I may say it is not the proper way to promote goodwill between the citizens of a country. I may add that by cancelling the decision of the former government to build this penitentiary institution, public money has been used to try to promote in a partisan way the interests of a political party which is becoming more and more unpopular among the people.
I am looking forward to the day when the population of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, and more particularly that of St. Pie, will have an opportunity to prove publicly to the government what they think about its administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I still maintain what I said, but nevertheless I consider the speech of the hon. member to contain a very serious charge of discrimination against himself and the hon. members for Prince

Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), and Bow River (Mr. Woolliams).

Mr. Chairman, I maintain the charge I have laid. The fact that penitentiaries have been built in three or four ridings does not mean that there has been no injustice in my own constituency. I still contend that serious injustice has been committed against the people in my riding.
Mr. Chairman, last week the Minister of Justice was in Quebec helping to set up a committee when several members, including the Leader of the Opposition, discussed-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want to raise a question of privilege here, but last week I was not in Quebec. I was detained here throughout last week by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.

I am sorry; the minister was not in the house, then, when the matter of moving the federal women's prison to Cornwall was discussed. I thought he was taking part in the setting up of the committee, but perhaps he wishes to dissociate himself from that frustrating week-that is, a frustrating week in Quebec, not here.
However, I want to discuss this change in the location of the women's prison. I want to do so calmly, and I want to do so factually. The relocation was announced as a "gift to the people of Cornwall" by the former member for Laurier, Hon. Lionel Chevrier. I think anyone interested in penology or penitentiary reform was as disappointed as I was, and I am sure all hon. members were, at this change of direction in the penitentiary service. I want to make a comment or two about it.
It has been suggested that this was a blatant example of pork barrel politics. These descriptive words are not mine, as a matter of fact, but are from a Globe and Mail editorial on the subject. The Toronto Star puts it just as directly in an editorial on March 11 which is entitled, "The Patronage Prison". Both the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society have protested the Cornwall site in telegrams to the Prime Minister. I should like to quote from the Toronto Star editorial which says that the site is unsuitable on at least three grounds:
It is too far from the homes and families of the inmates, making visits an expense and a burden. The new prison would be 275 miles from Toronto where 33 of the present 122 inmates at the prison for women at Kingston formerly lived.
There are no Canadian universities or social research centres nearby. The nearest is Montreal, 75 miles away.
There are no psychiatric facilities nearby and no psychiatrists.
Supply-J ustice
The editorial goes on to make the following three points:
First, the minister could refer to the Archambault report on prisons which recommended that the jurisdiction over female prisoners should be entirely provincial so that they can be kept in prisons closer to their homes.
Second, rather than building one prison for all of Canada's female prisoners, three smaller prisons might be built, one in the west, one in Ontario and one in Quebec.
Finally, if the decision to build only one central prison is irrevocable, let there be a new women's prison at Kingston, where there has been a tremendous community interest in prison work, where there is a climate of social research and where the academic facilities are available.
I would like to submit that the decision to move to Cornwall was expedient politically but had no justification in good penology practice. It ignores a thoughtful review of criteria for prison location and structure by the Canadian corrections association, dated March 18, 1963. This association, which is a branch of the Canadian welfare council has this to say:
The Canadian corrections association is the national private organization that provides facilities for the inter-disciplinary study of problems associated with crime and delinquency, and for the exchange of information and ideas among those concerned with these major social issues.
The association's membership is made up of staff and board members of the wide range of services in this field: adult and juvenile, institutional and non-institutional, public and private; faculty members from the various university departments; and interested members of the public.
I do not suppose the former hon. member for Laurier was a member of the Canadian corrections association.
As part of its function, the association is directly interested in the developments in Canada's prison system that have occurred so rapidly in recent years-
I am going to interpolate here that this decision to go to Cornwall would be a direct contravention of the good practices set out in this blueprint. In its recommendations the Canadian corrections association has one statement of general principles that I would like to put on the record. It says:
Any building should be designed to serve the program for which it is intended. A prison should be designed to give expression to modem treatment concepts.
It further says:
An examination of what is involved in treatment is set out in the standard minimum rules for the treatment of prisoners and related resolutions adopted by the first United Nations congress on the prevention of crime and the treatment of offenders, August 30, 1955.
This group certainly would not approve any move to Cornwall on grounds of alleged expediency.
Prisons should be located within the limits or in the immediate vicinity of a major centre that has appropriate clinical facilities; it is an added

Supply-Justice
advantage if the centre also has a university. At the same time, it is desirable to avoid locations where the institution will be surrounded in a few years by a housing development.
The association lists several criteria, and I am going to read only the ones that are particularly germane to this prison.
1.	It should be in a location to attract and hold competent staff.
2.	An urban setting prevents the staff from becoming ingrown. This is a serious problem and, with all due respect to Cornwall, is one that might occur when the prison personnel are isolated, so to speak, from the stream of thought that would be provided in a location such as Kingston or a university centre.
3.	Community facilities, such as clinics, hospitals, technical schools, universities, etc., should be available, and it is again obvious that there is no university complex in Cornwall.
4.	The prison can be used for the field placement of university students, students in medicine, psychiatry, social work, psychology, law, sociology and theology. All these things are available in the city of Kingston but none of them mentioned in the list of criteria are available in the politically expedient location of Cornwall.
5.	The institution and the university can work together conveniently in research, and then there is the one I mentioned earlier that has been referred to by the editorial writers.
6.	Visiting by relatives of inmates is easier.
There is one other aspect of this criteria
blueprint that I would like to discuss, and that is the size. The Canadian corrections association says:
The appropriate size for an institution depends on the program and the type of inmate for which it is intended-
-but it should be-
-as small as possible.
Here is a perfect example where three small institutions across Canada could fit perfectly into the criteria set up by the best opinion in Canada.
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox participated in this debate the other day, and since then he has handed me a copy of a letter that the Kingston-Quinte branch of the Canadian association of welfare workers has sent to the Minister of Justice, dated March 30, 1964. I propose to make this letter part of the record:
Dear Sir:
The Kingston-Quinte branch of the Canadian association of social workers passed a unanimous motion at their last meeting that I should communicate to you our concern about the proposed move of the prison for women from Kingston to Cornwall. This group is composed of the majority of the professional social workers practising in

the counties of Frontenac, Lennox and Addington, Hastings and Prince Edward. Our concern in this matter is with the part played by adequately qualified professional staff in any program for the rehabilitation of the prisoners.
We are quite aware that the plant and facilities at the prison for women are not appropriate for their function and that a more suitable building or buildings might be provided in the future.
However, in face of considerable physical difficulties, the prison for women at Kingston has assembled a treatment staff which has made substantial improvement in the rate of recidivism of women drug addicts. This staff would be dispersed by such a move, and the very valuable experience of the after-care program which has been built up over many years, would be lost.
Again I am going to interpolate that I do not think this loss is worth the political expediency of the move.
One of the advantages of the present situation has been the availability of consultation with the university, which provides a school of law and of medicine, and the opportunity to take advantage of the very extensive psychiatric services available in this community. None of these advantages exist in Cornwall, and we think these matters are very important in deciding the appropriate location of such an institution, if the emphasis on a program of rehabilitation is to be continued.
I believe there are very careful statistics available to document the improved outcome of the present treatment program, which should be given serious consideration. We think it is appropriate as a professional body, to bring this aspect of the situation to your attention.
The letter is signed, "Elizabeth J. Grey, B.A.,	M.S.W., President, Kingston-Quinte
branch, Canadian association of social workers".
Here we have three groups, divorced as it were from the daily political activities of certain people, the Canadian welfare council, the Canadian corrections association and the Canadian association of social workers who make a compelling case against this change, and I urgently request the minister to follow the lead of a former minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Fulton, and recognize that in penology, as in many other aspects of our activities, the winds of change blow.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-88, to amend the British North America Act, 1867 (abolition of the Senate).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the House of Commons for the opportunity this afternoon to move the second reading of this bill, which would seek to amend the British North America Act in such a way as to abolish the Senate. I am grateful to the house, I may say, for the decision made yesterday on first reading, although I confess I was surprised that an attempt was made to prevent a member from introducing a bill. However, this attempt was overcome by a majority vote, in line with the tradition of this parliament whereby leave to introduce a bill is automatic, followed by first reading so that members may have the opportunity to read the printed bill and to see what it is all about.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I think the hon. member, knowing the rules so well, will appreciate that comment on a vote held on a previous occasion is not permissible.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that welcoming a vote on a previous day is hardly out of order. I am also delighted, as a result of the discussion which took place yesterday, that the house agreed unanimously to permit this bill to be placed at the top of the list of public bills and thus be called for second reading today. As I listened to the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday, when he gave on his party's behalf unanimous consent, and as I read those words in Hansard, I felt he had committed this house to a moral obligation. He said that he and his party were prepared to give the required unanimous consent so that members of the house could stand up and be counted as to where they stand on this legislation. Therefore I feel that hon. members, having agreed to the debate this afternoon, are under a moral obligation to permit this bill to come to a vote and that they should not engage in talking it out. If that should happen, or if that should be threatened, I trust that at six o'clock there will again be unanimous consent to this bill's retaining its position at the top of the list.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Yes.

Does he consider that
within the sphere of one hour there can be an exhaustive discussion of this important bill?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I recognize the difficulty of this being accomplished within one hour, but those were the terms stated by the Leader of the Opposition when he agreed to unanimous consent yesterday. I think either one of two things should be done. Either a vote should be allowed before six o'clock, or else more time should be permitted so that a vote can be taken on this issue. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that this bill should not be talked out but that arrangements should be made so that members can stand up and be counted, giving an indication as to where they stand on this issue.
I also want to express the hope that on this very important issue we might have, in all parties if you please, what is sometimes referred to as a free vote. In other words, I hope we will not necessarily divide along party lines; and in particular if there are those on the government side who feel that they cannot vote for the principle of this bill by voting yes on second reading, that the other members on the government side will be free to vote for it if that is their view.
I want to say quite readily, Mr. Speaker, that I gave notice last Friday night of the introduction of this bill and I have brought it in at this time because the whole question of the Senate as a part of our parliamentary set-up has been brought into sharp focus by recent events. But it is not only because of recent events that I have introduced this bill. As hon. members know, the proposed abolition of the Senate is in the platform of the New Democratic party, and apparently I shall have to send a copy of the platform to a friend of mine in the other place who was under a misunderstanding last night.
As hon. members also know, many of us in all parties in Canada-and I can tell that this is so from the telegrams and messages I am getting at this time, many of which are from both Liberals and Conservatives-feel that this is a fundamental issue: Should our parliament have in it a body which has an equal say with the elected representatives, when the members of that body are not elected and are not responsible to the people of this country?
That is the basic issue. Are we really a democracy? Do we stand by the principle that the laws of a country should be made only by those who are elected by the people? If I make a mistake in this House of Commons, or if I vote the wrong way, or if I hold up parliament, I am responsible to the people of Winnipeg North Centre. I have to go back to them at the next election and face their

judgment. But a gentleman in the other place can stand up and do something which does damage to many people across the country, and he is responsible to no one, not even to the person who recommended his appointment to that place. I suggest that there is a basic inconsistency in that position and that in this day and age our parliament should consist only of those who are elected by the people and who are responsible to them.
It is sometimes argued-in fact it is put up as the last argument for the retention of a non-elected second chamber in our parliament -that this was part of the original arrangement and was provided as a protection for minorities, particularly as a protection for the provinces of this country as such. I think the answer to that is to ask what the Senate has done to protect the rights of the provinces. What has the Senate done to protect minorities in this country? Any protection that has been provided either to the provinces or to the minorities of this country has been provided by parliament as a whole, through legislation emanating from this elected House of Commons, or by the courts.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, despite the fact that on first reading no debate was possible, certain debate did arise on a point of order, so that we have been given a preview of some of the arguments against this bill. One of the arguments made was that the bill is unconstitutional; that we do not have the right to amend our constitution in this way. You sir, in my view made a proper ruling when you indicated that it was not the function of the Chair to rule on constitutionality. After all, sir, if you started doing that your life would be a busier one than it is already.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Could he tell the house what hopes he anticipates his bill has of passing the Senate?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I am coming to that in a minute if my hon. friend will let me. As I was saying, the question of deciding on the constitutionality of every piece of pension legislation or family allowance proposal, or anything of that nature, is surely not a function for Your Honour but must be a function for the courts.
It is my submission that under section 91A of the British North America Act parliament has the right to amend our constitution with respect to matters exclusively federal. We do from time to time amend our constitution as to the representation in this house among the provinces. We have taken steps to try to amend the constitution with respect to the qualifications of senators. I submit that this is a federal matter and that we have the right to make such an amendment in parliament.
British North America Act
It has been suggested as part of the argument against this bill that it is unilateral; that it is an attempt on our part, on the part of the House of Commons, to abolish the other place. I thought we had the reductio ad absurdum when it was suggested that, if that is the case, the Senate could bring in a bill to abolish the House of Commons. Surely it should be clear to all members that this is not a unilateral action on our part. This is a bill which to become law would have to be passed by this house and the Senate, and would then have to receive royal assent; so it is not unilateral action but parliamentary action.
Would the hon. member allow a question. Would it not also require the consent of the provinces?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That question is an assertion by the Leader of the Opposition, backed by some of his supporters. I am equally entitled to make the assertion that under section 91A it is not necessary to have the consent of the provinces to amend the constitution with respect to matters which are exclusively federal. Indeed, I ask the Leader of the Opposition, did he get the consent of the provinces before he proposed to amend the British North America Act with respect to the age of senators?
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am asking the Leader of the Opposition, who is making no reply.

Will the hon. member permit this question? Does he not recognize a difference between abolition and a change in age? So far as the provinces are concerned, is there not a difference between whether a senator is 74 years and 11 months or 76 years old and whether the Senate is to be abolished entirely? The whole question of abolition goes to the root of the constitution of the country.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I think the direct answer to the hon. member's question is no; it would not make any difference to a province so far as those two points are concerned. I have to watch my time, Mr. Speaker, for I have only 20 minutes. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) wants to know whether I think the Senate will pass this bill. I do not imagine that the Senate would pass this bill, certainly in today's atmosphere, if this house were to pass it, but I say to him and to the country that if the House of Commons passes a bill like this and the Senate defeats it, and if the House of Commons passes it again and the Senate defeats it, and if this goes on, and then there is an election, the Senate will

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That of course is nonsense. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are not on the clauses of the bill, but this is a very important point that the hon. member has raised. In so far as the bill amends any of the sections of the British North America Act other than the first one it amends, it does so consequentially. It does it only by taking out references to the Senate. The amendment to section 133 of the British North America Act makes no change of substance in section 133 as it now stands. All it does is to delete references to the Senate, the Senate having already been abolished by an earlier clause of my bill.
The hon. member knows this will set a precedent-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The hon. member knows I have only 20 minutes. It has been said in various ways that we have no right to take this action. In reply to that I should like to 

point out that at least two of the provinces of Canada have taken by themselves the kind of action that is proposed in this bill. I have in my hand a copy of chapter 28 of the statutes of the legislature of Manitoba for 1876. To go back to 1870 when Manitoba was constituted, it then had two houses, a legislative council and a legislative assembly, but by act of the legislature in 1876, which I have here, the upper house was abolished and the legislature of Manitoba was declared to consist of the lieutenant governor and the legislative assembly.
In the same way the province of Nova Scotia in the session of the legislature in 1928, that recently if you please, passed an act which abolished the legislative council and amended the constitution of the province. The Leader of the Opposition said yesterday that my bill would destroy parliament. That was a nonsensical observation. Manitoba did not destroy its legislature when it abolished the non-elected upper chamber; it strengthened the legislature. Nova Scotia did not destroy its legislature when it abolished its upper chamber; it strengthened the legislature. I suggest it would not destroy the parliament of Canada by one iota if we were to do away with the non-elected wing of it. We would be strengthening our parliament if we were to put it on the basis of complete parliamentary democracy.
Some hon. members have been saying that the House of Commons has been insulting the other place and my action has been characterized in certain ways. I could never say of the Senate what some people have said about it. There is just one quotation I should like to read. I will indicate its author, but I take it from page 339 of the book, "The Government of Canada", by MacGregor Dawson:
A senatorship isn't a job, it's a title. Also it's a blessing, a stroke of good fate; something like drawing a royal straight flush in the biggest pot of the evening, or winning the Calcutta sweep. That's why we think it wrong to think of a senatorship as a job; and wrong to think of the Senate as a place where people are supposed to work. Pensions aren't given for work.
The author of those words uttered in 1942 is the gentleman who is now the senator for Carleton in the other place, my friend Hon. Senator O'Leary. That same gentleman and others have talked about the dignity that should be accorded to the Senate. I say that dignity is not something you get by having it accorded to you. Dignity is something you earn, and the Senate of Canada has not earned dignity so far as the people of Canada are concerned by the way in which it has acted in the last few weeks. It certainly did not earn dignity when it delayed to 35,000 unemployed people in this country, even by one day, payment of their unemployment

insurance warrants to which they were entitled under legislation of this country.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
My hon. friends want to put the blame on the Liberals. I will join them in putting all kinds of blame on the Liberals for their delay, their bungling and mishandling of the business of the house. But when we got down to the wire and the last day had come and the money for the payment of these warrants was not available except by parliamentary action, I say that anyone in this house or in the other place who acted as the Senate did was indulging in most undignified action. What was done deserves the criticism that has been heaped on the other place.
Some people say to me: Is there not a place for people like those who are in the Senate? Is there not a job for them to do in our Canadian set-up? I think there is. I believe there are roles for elder statesmen. I think that the kind of job which some of the senators have done in working on committees that have studied unemployment, aging, land use and other subjects have been good, have been constructive and worth-while efforts. But it is one thing to engage in a piece of research, one thing to do a job for Canada that is helpful to the elected representatives of the people, and another thing to have at the same time the right of veto or the right of delay with regard to legislation passed in this house.
Most Canadians are not aware, of course, of the fact that the Senate, unlike the House of Lords at Westminster, unlike the president of the United States with their temporary veto power, can go on year after year to the end of time, if it wishes to do so, saying no to legislation passed in this house. I raise this not as criticism of my friends in the other place, and I have many friends over there. I have known many of them when they were in this house and they are still friends.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: They meet me in the hall and I have lunch with them and we can still talk. They know, even if my Conservative friends in this house do not, that what is being discussed now is not a matter of personalities but rather a basic principle of democracy, and in that light I think the day must come when Canada will have to do certain things to improve our parliamentary set-up. We have got improvements to make.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

That is why I ask the house to consider favourably this bill which will do what we have a right to do, amend our constitution so as to make our parliament consist, as my bill says, of the Queen and the House of Commons, an elected body with final authority to legislate on behalf of the people of Canada.

The hon. member referred to the veto year in and year out to the end of time. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The Senate vetoed the first old age pension bill and as far as I am concerned that is enough. It has vetoed several other measures as well. No parliamentary constitution should read in those terms. speechtext:
It is always a pleasure to take part in a quiet, friendly debate. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who introduced the bill neglected -I might say in a rather precipitate way-to explore the other avenues that might be open to him to achieve a more salutary performance in the upper chamber. He did not explore methods of reform. He did not explore the constitutional reforms available, nor the administrative reforms that might be discussed. Nor did he, I say with respect, deal with the constitutional problems involved in this bill and the practical consequences of it in terms of federal-provincial relations.
On reading the debates that preceded confederation, and the debates that preceded the London conference, I think it is quite clear that the purpose of the Senate was to preserve the territorial equality as between Upper and Lower Canada, and to preserve the rights of the maritimes. Anyone who takes the trouble to read those debates would find it an inevitable conclusion of such reading that neither Lower Canada nor the maritimes
1870	HOUSE OF
British North America Act would have come into confederation had the principle of equality of representation in the upper house not been achieved.
That being so, it is not merely a question of analysing section 91A of the British North America Act, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did yesterday. It is not merely a question of analysing whether the federal government, with the unanimous consent of the provinces, has jurisdiction to abolish or even reform the Senate. The question, rather, is a practical one: Whether in terms of today's Canada the abolition of the Senate, which has as one of its historical reasons and impulses the protection of territorial equality among the partners to confederation is practically possible. The question is whether the provinces to this confederation would consent to such abolition. Whether the constitutional matter is decided one way or another-and I would say there are grave doubts that section 91A of the British North America Act is wide enough within its purview to allow this bill-whether or not there is constitutional justification for it, certainly the provinces would probably take great exception to an elimination of this historic right.
I would refer the house to reports of the proceedings of the 1950 and 1951 federal-provincial conferences at which this question came up, and every province, except Saskatchewan, filed in the minutes of those proceedings their veto against the abolition or fundamental constitutional reform of the Senate without their consent. That is a matter of record in the historical documents of this country and one which the hon. member, I say with the greatest deference to his knowledge and experience, has failed to consider.
I will concede with him that in practical terms today the other place has not been the first bastion of provincial rights. The growth of the cabinet system, the way the cabinets have been chosen in Canada, representing various regions and ethnic groups, the fact that the courts have traditionally been the first protection, certainly constitutionally, of provincial rights, the fact that in terms of practical politics any federal government that persisted in acting to the detriment of any section of the country could not long survive -all this has made the traditional role of the Senate as a protector of provincial rights less valid. But, speaking in practical terms, the records of this country show that the provinces almost unanimously have objected to any step that would abolish the other place, and this is recorded in the minutes of the federal-provincial conferences.


Now, looking at the records too, may I refer to a speech made in Cobourg on January 28, 1957, during the election campaign of that epoch, when the Leader of the Opposition said to the people of Cobourg that his party promised to call a conference of the federal and provincial governments on reform of the Senate, if he were to become prime minister. I would like to read his words into the record:
We will convene a conference of the dominion and provincial governments and on the basis of its recommendations will make the Senate an effective instrument of parliamentary government.
May I ask the hon. member what date that was?

I would like to proceed with my argument. The basis of what I would like to say here is that the other place-and here we have a puzzle, what I once called a conundrum in this country-that the other place must either be given an opportunity of exercising a useful role in the parliamentary system, to exercise in Sir John A. Macdonald's own words, familiar enough to him, "a sober second thought" on legislation wherein he conceived the Senate would be the controlling or regulatory rather than the initiating branch of parliament, or it must cease to exist at all. Then, surely, and only then, would it be the duty of this house after a properly conceived and thorough debate to refer the question of reform to a federal-provincial conference. The problem as I see it is this: The other place is not given enough to do. Most of our legislation is introduced in this house as it has to be, under the terms of section 53, in respect of money bills. Most of the major bills brought before parliament

have to do with money and, in consequence, they are introduced here, debated at length, and finally referred to the other place only at a late stage in the parliamentary session.
At one time the composition of the cabinet used to include a member or two from the Senate. This is another role which has been minimized of late years and, in consequence, the other place is less useful than it might otherwise be. My suggestion is that we should seek to achieve administrative reforms which would allow important legislation to be introduced from time to time in the upper chamber for consideration there, particularly when such legislation was of a non-partisan nature or not too controversial. Either we should do this or we should proceed to a more fundamental reform along the lines indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The hon. member has himself recognized the validity and effectiveness of the Senate committee system. There is, I am sure it will be agreed, a non-partisan attitude taken toward legislation, and I should like to direct the attention of the house-
On a point of order, I think the time allowed to the hon. member has expired and that members of other parties should be allowed to express their views.

Yesterday I raised certain objections to this measure. I have now examined it in detail and listened to its proposer, and I am just as thoroughly convinced that this is a bad bill.
This bill does not seek to reform the Senate. This bill simply abolishes the Senate. This bill seeks drastically to alter the composition of the parliament of Canada. That is the issue before us today. We are not here to discuss reform of the Senate in any particular. This bill seeks to destroy parliament as we know it and as we have known it since confederation. I emphasize this particularly, because if the measure were aimed at the reform of the Senate there would be many matters which this house could discuss. It is generally agreed that the Senate could become more effective if a number of reforms were made. The official opposition has long been in favour of the reform of the Senate and has, in fact, brought forward resolutions in this
British North America Act regard. I would refer hon. members to Hansard, particularly to the reports of our debates in 1954, and suggest they read the speeches made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), and others, all dealing with the matter of Senate reform. Let us be perfectly clear. We are not discussing Senate reform today but the complete abolition of the Senate.
The official opposition unequivocally opposes this bill because it strikes at the roots of parliament. Parliament is composed of the Queen, the Senate and the commons. Passage of the hon. member's bill through this house would be as illogical and absurd as it would be to suggest that the Senate could, in its turn, legislate the House of Commons out of existence, and I repeat this, notwithstanding the glib phrases used by the proposer of the measure before us.
I would also bring this to the attention of hon. members: In accordance with the provisions of the British North America Act as it now stands, the three provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are given constitutional guarantees as to their representation in this house. We need only look at history leading up to confederation. Let hon. members consider the development of the western provinces which also received a bloc of 24 Senate seats. We had the Atlantic provinces, we had Ontario, we had Quebec and we had the western provinces. There is no one, and I include the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who can say it was not a basic condition of entry into confederation that the rights of the provinces would be protected through their equal representation by divisions in the Senate. Changes of population in the interval have, of course, affected the position. When the four western provinces were allocated their 24 Senators, their population was minute. In contrast the population of my own province today outnumbers the present population of the original maritime provinces. Well, we have six Senators to their 24.

Mr. Speaker, while I do not condone the situation that exists at the present time in the Senate, neither am I in favour of the abolition of the other place because I believe that if the Senate were properly reformed it could All a very useful and constructive purpose in our parliamentary system of government. That could be as a house of scrutiny, a house of second thought, a
British North America Act house from which we could draw many of our commissioners to deal with our public and governmental problems.
However, the Senate must be something more than a rubber stamp. If this house really expects the Senate to be nothing more than that, quite obviously it has become a very expensive rubber stamp and the bill we are now considering is an intelligent one. I would suggest, however, that what is wrong is not the fact that we have a Senate, but the shameful way in which both senators and the institution of the Senate have been treated by the present and past administrations of the old line party systems.
The Senate as we have it today is not that useful part of the government of Canada that was intended by the fathers of confederation. Instead it is a pasture for the political war horses of the old line parties who have outlived their strength and usefulness and are now put out to grass. It is a place, too often, to which the incompetent can be retired without disgracing the administration to which they once belonged. No wonder that a body composed in this manner commands little respect and that those members who try to discharge its function in a useful manner are flouted. Therefore I believe it is our responsibility at another time to debate intelligently and in a positive way methods by which the Senate can be reformed.
It is an indictment of our parliamentary system that in Alberta a Social Credit government for nearly 30 years, a C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan for 20 years, a Social Credit government in British Columbia for 12 years and, yes, a Union Nationale government in Quebec for 20 years have never been recognized; they have been ignored completely in this regard. I can think of an elder statesman who served in this house, who belongs to the party of the hon. member who moved this bill and who would make a very responsible and deserving senator if he were given that opportunity. I speak of M. J. Coldwell. Therefore I believe that in consultation with the provinces we ought to get together and reform the Senate and make it the useful body that it should be.

The second question I should like to ask the minister concerns a matter about which some people have also made representations to me. It involves a judge of the Quebec courts by the name of Ouimet who sentenced a man to jail for 12J months, I believe, for writing a letter to a newspaper criticizing a decision that the judge had made. So far as the composition and details of the firearms committee are concerned, I must say that I do not have same at my fingertips. I do not have the names of the members. It is an interdepartmental committee that has had several sittings. I have already begun to look into the reports of that committee and have been discussing same not with the members themselves, but through one of my officials in charge of the criminal law section. I have already made one answer in the house to the effect that, for the moment, there was no intention of curtailing the use of firearms. The only limitations that were under study, not considered for recommendation but under study were, (a) the possibility of increasing the age at which a person could use a firearm without being under the control of a responsible person and, (b), preventing the use of firearms by certain people, inter alia people already found guilty of offences against our laws.
As to the second point raised with regard to the sentence which has been imposed by Mr. Justice Ouimet, I must say that, like my hon. friend, I am not in a position to state exactly the duration of the sentence involved. However, I recall quite clearly that this was one case where a person, having read about a sentence which included the condemnation to lashing felt that this was an undue type of condemnation to impose and wrote a letter to the newspapers which could have been termed at least inflammatory. The person concerned was charged, with contempt of court, because the judge, in imposing sentence, had not gone beyond the scope of his jurisdiction under the code. The person had inferred, in the language used, that the judge had been wrong in applying the law.

There are two questions raised by this incident. The first one is connected with the administration of justice. This is, of course, purely a matter for the provincial government under the British North America Act. The second question is one which I hope we are not going to discuss fully here tonight, and that is the matter of the propriety of henceforth maintaining in the code provision for a sentence to lashing.
In so far as the replacement or retirement of incompetent judges is concerned, I must answer that the question of revolving judges either by districts or otherwise is one for the chief justice of each court. At a later date I want to make a rather full statement in connection with the question of penitentiaries administration and the particular problem of minimum security institutions. For the time being I should like the minister to comment on a matter that is very seriously concerning me, and several other people who are in the same situation. I refer to the general policy of the decentralization of penal institutions.
It has been long recognized that there are many inmates of institutions who can be rehabilitated. However, these people have to be segregated from the others and given training programs. It is a very difficult matter to put a program like this into effect. The public is far from sympathetic and there are failures even under this type of program. I believe that within the administration of the penitentiaries branch possibly there are people who doubt the advisability of minimum security institutions and the segregation of different classes of prisoners. It takes a strong government and a strong minister to lay down a policy in connection with prison reform and to carry it out. If he does not do this himself the program will begin to disintegrate.
I am concerned because of a feeling that two things are happening, and I hope the minister can ease my conscience about both these things. First, I am concerned that the policy that was instituted some years ago by Hon. Davie Fulton of decentralizing penal institutions into many smaller units and into maximum and minimum security institutions, is being abandoned. Then, I am concerned lest there is an effort on behalf of the government to phase out minimum security insti-
[Mr. FavreauJ
tutions now in existence. I have recently had evidence placed before me that at least one minimum security institution already in operation may be in the process of being closed. I refer to the Beaver Creek camp. This, I feel, would be a reversal of the policy which was begun a few years ago and which has been quite successful. This camp is very close to me, and I have seen it grow and operate. It was well started and has had a very good history of keeping people out of trouble after they have been released.
There are indications that this government is giving in to those people within the penitentiaries branch who are against this type of penal reform. It seems to me that over the last few months the efforts of the government have been very largely turned towards building institutions on a patronage basis. I do not want to go into all the things that have been said about the Cornwall institution and the institutions that were supposed to have been put in Grey-Bruce, St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, and so on. But it seems to me that the attitude of the previous minister, in the statements he made, was that the penitentiaries branch was merely considered by the government for building institutions in the ridings of its own members, and taking them out of the ridings of members of the opposition. In addition to that, it appears that some of the institutions that were planned, the minimum security institutions, are not only not being built in the ridings of opposition members but are not being built at all.
That program was started. It was successful, and I would like an assurance from the minister that he is firmly behind those people within his penitentiaries branch who support the minimum security institutions and the decentralization of prison farms and penitentiaries. I have a fairly extended speech prepared but I do not want to delay the estimates unduly. However, this is a matter I do not want to leave until we come to the main estimates. I want to be satisfied that the minimum security institutions system will be carried through and that the minister is wholeheartedly behind it. I ask the minister to give me such an assurance.

Mr. Chairman, while we are considering the estimates of the Department of Justice, I should like to say that I am particularly disappointed to see that the minister has not provided special items which would permit the government to launch a full inquiry into bankruptcies occurring across the country, and particularly in the province of Quebec, where the situation is becoming increasingly alarming-

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It is perhaps a bit unfortunate that this matter has been raised from time to time. It is certainly a difficult point to rule upon, but in the opinion of the Chair there was, when we originated this discussion earlier in committee of supply, an understanding of some nature-I really cannot tell how far it went-that on the first item of each one of the departments where there is a general administration item there would be a discussion of a general nature. This has been my impression all along and this is why we have been following this procedure during the days while the supplementary estimates have been under consideration.
I point out that this does not mean we have suspended the ordinary rules of procedure in this committee. The general rules of relevancy still apply. Standing order number 59(2) still applies as does, of course, the citation from May which I quoted last night and which perhaps I should quote again for the benefit of hon. members. This reads:
Of course, it is quite obvious that it should be improper, as a general rule, to raise on a supplementary estimate the whole question of policy involved in the original estimate.
As I said last night, this is a general rule which we have to bear in mind even though

we have recognized that there can be a general discussion. In other words, my feeling is we have recognized that the committee may proceed with a general discussion on the first item where there is a general administration item. But the Chair should, I submit, rule on every particular intervention on its own merits so as to determine whether it follows the ordinary rules of relevancy which continue to apply, even in this debate.

I think that for the purpose of clarification I have to make two points. The first is that when we began this discussion on March 13 this committee was in unanimous agreement that we should proceed to a general discussion on the first item of the estimates of each department. There was no agreement confined only to general administration items. That agreement covered all departments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think we should go into the matter further. I said, and I feel my thinking is generous enough, that we should consider each intervention on its merits. I have studied all the observations which have been made. I have considered what I myself, said. If the hon. member for Yukon would go through all the comments which were made on the point of order originally raised by various members, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, he would see that it was the feeling of the members who brought up this point that there would be a general discussion where there was a general administration item. I think, in fact, that this would cover most of the departments; if my recollection is correct there are few whose estimates do not begin with a general administration item.
However, I do not think we should make a general ruling. We should consider each situation as it arises. In the present instance the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac has begun a discourse on the administration of bankruptcy. It would not be possible for the Chair to make a ruling on whether the hon. member is in order or not because I have not heard enough of his discourse and I invite him to continue his remarks for the time being.

Mr. Chairman, the Bankruptcy Act is inadequate, almost useless as far as its practical application is concerned, and the impact of this inefficiency is felt almost in all areas of business but especially, perhaps because of its more fragile nature, by small industry, by our small traders, which is very understandable indeed, large companies

being protected by lawyers who are expert in these matters, whereas the small trader, whoever he is, cannot afford to seek legal advice in view of the huge expenses involved.
The situation is such, Mr. Chairman-and I am certain that the minister, who is a brilliant lawyer, is aware of this-that Le Petit Journal for the week of March 15, 1964, published an article relating sensational revelations by a person in the know and entitled:
I worked in the fraudulent bankruptcy business.
That article describes the gigantic organization which controls this continuing fraud, and throws some light on the procedure used to entice tradesmen with financial problems to rush into the lion's mouth.
When newspapers have the courage to put before the population an article of this quality, it is hightime for legislators, and especially those who administer this famous act, to face up to their responsibilities and ask themselves frankly what changes are required in the light of recent events.
Mr. Chairman, may I quote in its entirety the introductory paragraph of this article, written by Mr. Conrad Bernier. It begins this way:
The season of the fat kine has been going on for some time for the experts in fraudulent bankruptcy. The number of their victims since a little over two years is unbelievable.
By its magnitude, by the strength and the complexity of its organization, the racket of fraudulent bankruptcies has taken such ugly, brutal and fantastic proportions that it is jeopardizing the entire local trade-
The author is referring to Montreal.
Allow me to mention to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) that as a small manufacturer, in Montreal only, out of ten customers to whom I sold goods, eight have gone bankrupt. I would therefore ask him to listen closely to this:
-which may be plunged in a complete chaos. The damages, states an eminent financier-
-and it is still Mr. Bernier who is writing-
-are huge and, faced with such gangsters, one feels very small, insignificant and lost. Those gangsters who hustle us and may even knock us down and squash us have corrupted and altered business to an extraordinary degree. The fraudulent bankruptcy racket has become an ever-spreading organization which must be hunted down and destroyed at all costs.
You can see as well as I do that those words leave no possible doubt as to the seriousness of the situation. Moreover, to assist him in his clean-up job, the Minister of Justice could surely rely on the solid support of his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), whose competence and integrity would undeniably be major assets in helping him take the pulse
Supply-Justice
of that situation, diagnose the disease and then apply the remedy required.
Reference was made to the setting up of a judicial committee or something of the kind in Montreal to have a look at the situation and probably submit a report which, like so many others, would wind up gathering dust in the departmental files.
The basic problem lies in the provisions of the act itself, and it is this act that should first be studied, revised, reviewed and amended. I intended to introduce a bill or a motion to that effect. I inquired of the house's legal adviser, but since he is overworked and that, according to him, such a revision would require almost a month's work and still, by a legal expert, it was considered almost impossible.
Only departmental officials can perform this work efficiently and officially, because questionings would no doubt be necessary. In fact, an entire legal machinery should be set up so as to throw some light on this unsavoury business that reeks of fraud and which our honest businessmen are practically unable to avoid, being blinded by a doubtful legality that leaves room for quibbling and interpretation by any sharp swindler.
Last year the minister of justice gave me several documents concerning bankruptcies following a question I had put on the order paper. Along with those statistics, some of which I will give in a few moments, I could read the following paragraph:
Who assumes the losses presumably suffered according to the figures given in those charts? The records at the office of the superintendent of bankruptcy do not give the total number of claims filed by the creditors, except when a dividend is declared. Consequently, the figures for the liabilities are those given by the debtors themselves and are only an estimation. Furthermore, when the secured creditors take back their securities, unless they give the amount really recovered, only an estimation based on the value of the securities can be made.
According to information available, we cannot distinguish between secured, preferred and unsecured creditors and determine the loss apparently sustained by each category.
It follows from this answer of the minister that the administrators of this act are as inefficient as the act itself.
A lot of technicalities are put forward and it is hardly possible to succeed with antiquated methods. Meanwhile, people who have devoted their whole life to building up a business, witness failure of their most legitimate ambitions and loss of the little they own because an inefficient act is unable to prevent swindlers from grasping their belongings.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to quote a few figures in support of my remarks. In 1958,

in cases of non-summary proceedings, the estimated liabilities of debtors amounted to $34,330,098, and in cases of summary proceedings-
