Estimated liabilities of debtors totalled $34,330,098 and, on summary conviction, $10,062,138. Those figures have kept on increasing since 1958 and have reached a point where, according to 1962 statistics, liabilities on non-summary conviction were $69,989,460 and $10,749,735 on summary conviction. Gentlemen, the present avalanche of bankruptcies will no doubt reach new records for the last fiscal year.
I will just give you the total amount of apparent losses for 1962; on non-summary conviction, they totalled $15,695,662 and $5,779,801 on summary conviction. And, as the Minister of Justice stated in the quotation I read at the beginning of my remarks, because of the present provisions of the law, it is extremely difficult to determine those losses with a normal degree of precision. Consequently, those figures are but a poor indication of an unfortunate situation and I will be happy to provide the information I have to anyone who wishes to examine the question.
To conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister the following question, and I would appreciate it if, with his usual courtesy, he would take it into serious consideration: would the Minister of Justice be prepared to make an inquiry into these fraudulent bankruptcies? In addition, would he be prepared to establish a committee or another

body to study immediately the possibility of revamping the Bankruptcy Act. Finally, is the Minister of Justice ready to assume responsibility for instituting a temporary commission to scrutinize all bankruptcy cases, especially in Montreal and in the province of Quebec, until a preliminary report from the said commission has been submitted to his department?
Something must be done, for the situation has become tragic in several places; and the business community is becoming panicky, for it knows very well that the law, though existing, no longer protects them adequately.
Mr. Chairman, some tradesmen who have suffered from this situation asked me on several occasions whether there was in Ottawa a minister of justice or a minister of injustice. I would not go so far as calling the hon. member the minister of injustice, but if the situation in regard to bankruptcies continues and if the government and the Minister of Justice fail to face up to their responsibility, this will finally happen.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to briefly draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that recently the Department of National Defence announced the closing down of the radar station at St. Sylvestre. There is at that place an immense site on which the Department of Justice could base some projects.
On the other hand, I have been informed, that the Department of Justice was interested in that site which, will be vacant in July, since the radar station will then be closed.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the vacancy of that site at St. Sylvestre, if he has any projects for some rehabilitation institution, because he could establish some very beneficial institutions there.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a few remarks to the Minister of Justice in connection with some letters I have received from presidents of rifle clubs. I have one in my possession from the Coleman rifle and revolver club, Mr. John W. Dean. I have another from the Okotoks shooting club, from the president Mr. Denis Gough. I have many others in my file which I have referred to the minister, but up to now I have not received what seems to me a satisfactory explanation of either his views or the views of his government with regard to bringing forward legislation to restrict the use of firearms by private citizens. Some of these clubs fear that some irresponsible legislation might be brought forward by the justice department concerning the ownership and use of firearms

by private citizens. In essence their views, with which I agree, are that they do not think that further legislation, would be of any value, to unarm the irresponsible gunman.
I should like to add that when you go to outlying spots in western Canada the use of firearms is even encouraged among juniors. May I cite to the Minister of Justice an experience I had last summer at Aklavik in the Northwest Territories where the principal of the school conducted target practice in the basement of the school, teaching children the science of using firearms so that they might become skilled in shooting muskrats on the Mackenzie river delta. The same thing happened among the Indians at Old Crow. It is nothing uncommon to see young people in the west using 22's and other firearms to shoot gophers, and so on. I think it is a fine thing for these young people to gain experience, and the justice department should be encouraging them, rather than restricting the use of firearms and bringing forward legislation to this effect.
May I have the attention of the minister, because I am talking to him direct; it is his department which is concerned. I hope that he in turn will pay proper heed to these requests which are coming in from different gun clubs, and I trust he will think seriously before making any move to introduce further legislation to restrict the use of firearms in the hands of private citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up a lot of time on these supplementary estimates, but there are one or two matters which I wish to draw to the attention of the minister. This is the first time we have had some of the estimates from the Department of Justice under consideration by the house for a matter of many months, so there is some justification on these supplementary estimates to probe a little deeper into the administration of this and other departments than is normally the case on supplementary estimates. Many of the estimates for the 1963-64 fiscal year were brought in prior to adjourning for Christmas, and in order to wind up the session some went through with less than one day's debate on the whole department. I think we should have an end to this criticism of members of the opposition who wish to bring up certain of these matters, because I would remind you that some of these matters we have had to keep to ourselves for more than two years.
I should like to ask the minister whether there is still a large backlog of cases before the Exchequer Court of Canada, particularly those concerning income tax appeals and matters of that kind. If there is, there is certainly something to this idea that justice
Supply-Justice
delayed is justice denied. I know one or two cases where income tax appeals have been placed before the Exchequer Court of Canada more than two years ago and a decision has not yet been handed down. I think it is time to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that if this court is unable to cope with the volume of work coming before it something should be done to expand its facilities, or some other kind of arrangement should be made so that some decisions can be reached with regard to these appeals.
As I said, I did not want to take up a lot of time but this is something that has been troubling a lot of citizens of Canada for a long period. Therefore I hope the Minister of Justice will have something to say with regard to expediting these cases which have been before the exchequer court for months, and in some cases for years.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this matter. The matter under discussion here is the printing of debates. I am not sure which minister is responsible for that item to the house.
I wonder whether, before proceeding with our observations, the house leader should not tell us which minister of the government is responsible for the item now before us.
It is Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Chairman, I understand it is the Speaker of the house himself.
On that matter, I should like to draw the attention of the house on the fact that the French version of the debates of the house are often late in reaching us so that, on many occasions, we have to come to the floor of the house for the next day's sitting without having received a copy of the order paper in French and without a copy of the debates.
Only today the same thing happened again; we did not receive the French copy of the order paper.
Yes.
We did not receive the French copy today, but-
Yes, I had it in my office.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there must be privileged people-
It was in my post office box.

-who receive it before some others.
The same thing happens for the French translation and printing of committee reports.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that you should report to the Speaker to that effect and ask him to bring about some improvements.
I know that there is a lack of reporters, interpreters, translators, etc., and I believe we have been complaining about that for two years in the house.
I feel the time has come for the government to take the necessary steps and see to it that French translations, French printings of committee reports, French editions of the order papers, of Votes and Proceedings and of the official record of the debates are made available to us at the same time as the English versions.
This is an important point, because it makes it more difficult for us when we receive them late.
Another point which I would like to mention, Mr. Chairman, and of which we had a
typical example this evening___and this could
perhaps be an important suggestion-is that a moment ago, the Minister of Justice referred to a page of Hansard. It was the English pagination, which is not the same as the French one.
It often happens that hon. members refer us to such and such a page of Hansard. I then look in the French copy of Hansard. Or when someone speaks in French and then the hon. members only have the English copy, they are rather lost because the pagination is not the same as on their English copy.
For instance, page 876 quoted tonight in the English version will probably be page 875 or still page 900 in the French version.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether house officials could not find means to use the same pagination in the English as well as in the French version of Hansard.
It is impossible.

Some rather difficult problems will have to be overcome no doubt in order to achieve this result, but I think it would be worth while.

Sometimes I quote an extract from Hansard and several members are unable to refer to it, because my quotation is according to the French pagination, while some members only have the English edition on their desks. The same thing happens when English speaking members quote pages from the English Hansard, while I have in my hand the French copy.
So, on this item, I think that I am in order when I make this suggestion. The officers of the house who are in charge of the English and French versions of Hansard should be asked to see that the page numbers are exactly the same in both editions, English and French.
It might simply be a matter of skipping some page numbers in the English version, since the French version is always longer. It might also be a matter of putting less matter on each page in the English version. Perhaps the form and size of the pages in the French edition should be enlarged. At all events, I think this is a problem for which it might be worth while to provide a solution.
I leave it to the staff of the house. I hope other hon. members will be just as interested to have the same page numbers in both editions used by all hon. members. Finally, I would very much like to see the matter considered so that a solution may be found.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to the suggestion or the request by the hon. member for Lapointe, he might perhaps be so kind, when proceeding with his research and finding the page in the English copy of Hansard, also to tell the house the corresponding page number in the French text. In this way, it would make things easier, and the problem would be automatically solved.
Mr. Chairman, it might be done in the majority of cases; indeed, I can well recall having done so on various occasions.

But the problem is this: For instance, as it happened early this evening, when the Minister of Justice quoted the page number in the English version, he obviously had no time to find out the French page number owing to the speed of proceedings. Those are the very circumstances in which my suggestion would prove most valuable.

matter of French translation and French publications appears to some to be in the process of being eliminated by his leader and by the leader of the government. If matters develop as they appear to be doing in some of our provinces it may be that this will not be a problem very long. It should also be borne in mind that the problem was not much of a one for many years but has grown in magnitude recently.
I think the Speaker should be in the house tonight because we are dealing with items under legislation for which he is responsible. I am surprised how little action has been taken with regard to the problems raised by many members of the house the last time we were discussing these estimates. It seems to me, and I have said this before, that there should be better arrangements than we have in relation to the staff of the house.
The other day I asked whether or not the staff were going to be paid for the statutory holidays of Good Friday and Easter Monday. I understood this matter was receiving consideration. It is not good enough, Mr. Chairman, to grant the staff a day off. This is not the accepted practice of organized labour and I do not believe parliament should foist it off on the people who work for this institution merely because they are unorganized. The general principle is that if statutory holidays are worked they are paid for with double time. I suggest the government should give immediate consideration to paying the staff for these two days that were worked through no fault of the staff themselves.
I feel this matter should not have to be raised continually. The government should do this, at least if they believe in normal labour relations. I have had a number of complaints recently from several departments with relation to vacation pay. Since the employees of the House of Commons are now on an almost yearly basis and no longer truly temporary, I believe it is necessary for the government to consider this matter. Really, it is the responsibility of the Speaker as chairman of the internal economy committee. It is his responsibility to see that vacation pay is granted. The suggestion is made that the staff will have time off and be paid for the time off. This is not the same thing, Mr. Chairman. The annual vacation with pay period should be a period in which the employee can choose which week or two weeks he will be on holiday and will be paid for it. This is the normal procedure in business and certainly should be the normal procedure in government.
The last time this item was discussed, we were told that the translations branch of the House of Commons were being treated

Supply-Legislation
disgracefully. There may be some explanation for what happened last week because it was generally understood there would be an Easter recess. However, during that week, as hon. members are aware business continued here and the members of the translation branch were divided between here and Quebec city. There were more members of our house translations staff in Quebec city than there were in the house. This meant that the normal rest periods provided for translators under international agreements in almost every other country of the world did not apply to Ottawa. I think this is a disgrace. The responsibility rests directly on the shoulders of the Speaker, who has done nothing about the problem although he is well aware of it.
There is another problem that has developed in relation to the cafeteria in the west block. This is a lovely building, but the men and women working in the cafeteria are on a split shift basis. They have a wash room in which they have to spend the two and a aalf hours between shifts, and it is not as big as the normal wash room in this building. This is not a rest room. If this room were in any other place some trade union officer would go to the Ontario government under the factories act and would be able to get better quarters than they have there now. I suggest that the Speaker take a look at the men's and women's wash rooms and then take a look at the room that is going to be the carpenter shop. It is a very attractive room and should be made the rest room for the staff in the west block, because it is adjacent to the wash room.
It seems surprising, Mr. Chairman, a member of parliament has to speak about these matters every time these estimates are before the committee. It seems to me that the Speaker has failed to do this job because he is not provided with the necessary people to tell him what the situation is. These matters should not have to be raised every time these estimates are before us. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, that some of the employees in the cafeteria receive the grand sum of $172 per month? This is less than a dollar an hour. No wonder the Liberal government has not agreed to put in a statutory minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. We do not pay our kitchen staff that kind of money. The take home pay of these employees is slightly over $120 and comes to a total of $170 with their meals. These people work on a split shift basis and have two and a half hours off in the afternoon. They leave at eight o'clock at night and they arrive here in time to make breakfast in the morning. I hope I do not have to raise this

matter again, and that the Speaker or whoever is responsible will do something about it.
There are, of course, many other problems that affect this house. We are not in a very healthy state in so far as our relations with our ridings are concerned. I think it is generally conceded that what has happened in parliament the last little while has not improved the stature of parliament. There has been the question of the need for the elimination of the other place because they hold up these bills.
What about you on divorce?

In my opinion, if the Liberal party had the gumption they would be justified in going to the electorate. The bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could easily be passed here, and then if it was turned down by the other place this would be a good election issue. Whether or not the method we use in this house is a satisfactory one from our point of view, it is certainly not satisfactory to the general electorate. I am sure that the majority-
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
I sincerely ask him this question. Does he feel the people of Canada want an election right now?

I am certain the people of Canada do not want an election right now. The reason they do not, Mr. Chairman, is that there is not going to be any change in this mess unless some of us who really believe in the democratic process are willing to make some changes in the system we use.
I think it is very difficult for a constituent to look at his member of parliament and say, "I am in communication with him, and what I suggest to him will finally be given a hearing in the house". How can anyone really say this to a backbencher of some of the political parties that have been in this house during the last 20 years? Tonight another member and I were discussing a certain gentleman who is never here. How would his constituents know whether or not he is here? How are they going to make an impression on him? How are they going to bring to his attention the needs that they may have.
It is necessary for us to make changes in our system. These changes have been brought about in other countries. The governments of few countries run their business as haphazardly as we do. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned a few minutes ago, this is the first opportunity we have had in a long time to discuss the Department of

Justice. I think we will all agree that we have abused the privilege of discussing supplementary estimates. Certainly many of the discussions we have been having should not take place on supplementary estimates. However, from the point of view of a member of parliament, Mr. Chairman, on what other occasion can these discussions take place? Many of these estimates have not been before us for almost two years. It seems to me a member of parliament has to take advantage of every opportunity as it comes along. The government has an obligation to decide when that opportunity is going to occur. I suggest we take a look at what some of the other countries in the world are doing. Most of them do not have a formal arrangement. They do not come to a deadline like Christmas and you will remember, Mr. Chairman, last year people cancelling their plane reservations because we were going beyond the day of adjournment for Christmas.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but for the last few minutes he has been straying from the item before the committee. On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, this is a matter of the operations of the house, and legislation is the item which is under consideration. We are now dealing with administration, which is the general item covering operations of the house, and I suggest these matters are relevant. It is no use referring to the committee, because it has been a complete washout in so far as solving the problems that come under the general administration of legislation. In England, for instance, they have been trained to the idea of having set periods of time in the operations of the house of commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the hon. member's information it has. It has been sitting and has actually made its first report to the house.
It still does a very poor job. I would suggest-
I would suggest you sit down.
The hon. member says sit down. That is all he ever does and he is getting broad across the beam from sitting.
I would rather be broad across the beam than be broad across the head.

The hon. member makes a better speech sitting down than he does standing up. If ignorance were a criterion he would be a very good member of parliament.
The matter of the relationship between a member of parliament and his constituency will have to be considered or parliament itself will reach a very serious impasse. It seems to me that the general administration item of this department is the one under which this matter should be considered. However, I will bow to your direction, Mr. Chairman, but I hope that some of the other matters I have raised in relation to the staff will be given very serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I will not be very long but, after the few remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I would like to give my side of the story. He says that we have been asking for our rights, as far as the French language is concerned, in the last few years only. Let us reverse the situation in the house for 24 hours only. Let us speak French only and let the English speaking element use the facilities put at our disposal in some committees.
The hon. member for Timiskaming is complaining because the hon. member for Lapointe wants to have identical page numbers in the French and English versions of Hansard. If we wanted to go further, as far as bilingualism is concerned, we should have a truly bilingual Hansard, that is to say the English version on one half of the page and the French version on the other. It would be a really bilingual book since each page would be written in the two official languages of the country.
When Hansard is printed solely in French, it is French; when it is printed in English only, it is English. I fail to see there any bilingualism.
Mr. Chairman, a truly bilingual book must have both languages on the same page, one

Supply-Legislation
alongside the other, so that it can be read in both English and French.
What is bilingualism? The French Canadian citizen is not always insisting on his rights without rhyme or reason, but he is always given the cold shoulder. That has always been detrimental to the French Canadians and we are asserting our rights.
In conclusion, let us take, for instance, Beauchesne's standing orders-
They are not the standing orders.

There has always been only an English edition. How can we uphold our rights when we do not even have these regulations in our own language and we cannot learn them?
When we are provided with a French edition of standing orders, we can assure you that when we rise to speak, Mr. Chairman, we will be in order.

Before this item passes, Mr. Chairman, I have one observation to make and it arises out of the role of the member of parliament. I think the best thing I can do is quote from an article in the Montreal Star of January 30, 1964.
Turner says M.P.'s power-

speechtext: Order. I again hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but it seems to me this would be out of order if he is discussing the role of members of parliament under this item. That might be quite right, except for one thing, that by the remarks I have made I may have misinterpreted what I had in mind. I would like to quote from this article which says:
Turner says M.P.'s power now a myth.
Liberal member of parliament John Turner, urging an overhaul of house procedures, yesterday called for the return of the power and influence of the individual M.P. which is now a "myth."
Addressing a meeting of the McGill University Liberal club, Mr. Turner, himself a relative newcomer to the political scene-condemned what he termed the "Monopoly of information," and challenged that the bureaucracy-"that mandarin class of faceless experts, protected by the cloak of anonymity of a government department, operating beyond the range of the people's control"-is fighting a running battle with members of parliament.
"The M.P.," he said "is losing that battle with the civil service."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Order. This comment is obviously out of order. Certainly what the hon. member is quoting now, and the remarks he is making, could not by any stretch of the imagination be considered to come

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I have a few remarks yet to make, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to read from a newspaper article the words-

I understood, Mr. Chairman, that, you were about to ask if I intended to rise on a point of order. I was not. I agree I may not get very far in my remarks-

speechtext: Then, I would say that after hearing the hon. member for a minute or two, and being generous with him, I ruled that his remarks were not pertinent to the resolution before the committee. Perhaps he would look for another occasion upon which to make his contribution.

Well, in view of the hour, and other things, I will be glad to bow to that ruling though I do feel-and I say this in all sincerity-that my remarks, and the others I was about to make had a direct bearing on the matter which is now before the committee.

I had intended to deal with somewhat the same subject matter as my hon. friend from Timiskaming. I had intended to refer to the public dissatisfaction which exists with respect to the House of Commons, its members, its activities and our participation in them, and to suggest ways in which we might conduct ourselves in a better manner.
Hear, hear.

These are things we should be trying to do here, in order to deal with public business in a manner which is fair and reasonable and in keeping with our responsibilities. I think this is a matter of extremely vital concern. It would not have been raised by members from different parties within a brief period of time if it were not a matter of general concern to the public and to the members of this house. I think this is one of the things we should be doing-discussing among ourselves and searching for ways and means of making the operation of this parliament effective.
It is true we have abused the procedures of this house. We have abused the rules as they apply to the consideration of the very estimates which are now before us, and I have participated in that abuse.

Shame.

speechtext: Order. I think when I consider the remarks which are now being made by the hon. member for Skeena in the light of the observations which were made a moment or two ago by the chairman, I have to say to the hon. member that I cannot consider his remarks at this time as being relevant to the item in the estimates before us. I would ask the hon. member to adhere as closely as possible to the item under consideration. I recognize that there has been some leniency shown on the debate on the first item, but I think we still have to recognize the rule of relevancy and I ask the hon. gentleman to do that.

Mr. Chairman, if you will consistently-and I do not only mean yourself as an individual; I include the others who occupy the chair from time to time-if you would consistently and persistently enforce that rule of relevancy I would be the first to support you. But, so far, this has not happened. Unfortunately, what has occurred is that there has been laxity allowed in debate on some items and constriction enforced with respect to other items. This is most unfair to members of the committee and it leaves open the question whether or not the degrees of rigidity or licence allowed on any particular item depend upon the quarter of the house in which the hon. members concerned sit. I know that is not so, but that question does occur and that is, particularly, why I went as far as I could in my remarks a moment ago so as to run foul of the rules, which I knew you had in the back of your mind, and which you were intending to use.
I am asking now, Mr. Chairman, for the orderly conduct of the business of this committee. I know you cannot speak for others who may occupy the position of chairman, but I am asking that you use, persistently, the heaviest possible gavel and crack down on all members who offend against the rules of relevancy, whether they happen to come from this quarter of the house, in the N.D.P. group, or whether the offender happens to be the Leader of the Opposition, or anybody else. If you will do that, you will find me the very first to support you all the way down the line.
My hon. friend behind me says: "Do it right away". I will do it right away by sitting down and let us hope I do not have to raise too many points of order about other people being out of order.

There is one other point on this item which I should like to raise. It

has to do with private members' bills. Since this government came to office bills which had been drawn up with the assistance of the assistant law clerk have from time to time been thrown out, when further study had been given to them after the Speaker had received them. I should like to persuade the minister of the desirability of providing for the assistance of the law officers so that when a bill has been drawn up by them for an hon. member and brought before parliament there shall be no question at that time with regard to whether or not the measure is fit to be presented to parliament. Surely, that is not too much to ask in the House of Commons of Canada. There could be a little saving if the proper scrutiny were given to the bills hon. members want to bring before the house prior to their being presented in the house. I just want to leave that thought with the government, because it is a practice that has grown up since this government came into office.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to belabour this point before the committee for very long, but as I came back into the chamber I noticed that the committee was on the legislation item and I do want to raise a point here that I am sure will be in order. I notice that this item involves the publishing of debates, and the next item is "Printing of other publications". I want to make a protest regarding the printing of Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day. The reason I am making the protest is that there is distortion of questions by the various bureaus, whatever they may be, of the Speaker's department; that is, distortion of the questions that hon. members place on the order paper. This distortion causes the question to lose its democratic value out in the country and area to which the question applies. If an hon. member puts a question on the order paper, provided it is not, as we often hear Mr. Speaker say, argumentative, controversial or improper, I think it should be sustained as it is written.
I will give the committee an example. Last March 24 I put a question on the order paper regarding the mails of Canada. The question was directed to the department of the Postmaster General and referred to the mails in the county of Prince Edward. I submit, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that it certainly had a democratic, local interest, reason and value. The question read as follows:
When will the Postmaster General open a post office in Rednersville, in Prince Edward county, in accordance with agreement to do so made with me by his predecessor last November?
I was giving the former postmaster general and the whole department the benefit of two

months, because when I got back to my files I found he had made the agreement with me last September, not last November as I had written in the question. Hon. members will find this question-distorted, of course- on page 31 of today's Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day. It was distorted by the bureau, or bureaus, as follows:
Did the Postmaster General, during November last, agree to open a post office in the village of Rednersville, Ontario, and, if so-
Imagine-"if so":
-When will such a post office be opened?
I had already told the Speaker and his bureau in my original question that the postmaster general had promised to open a post office in Rednersville. Mr. Chairman, I am sure you will agree with me that this is nothing but a flagrant distortion of a democratic question posed in the house for the benefit and in the interests of the constituents I represent in Rednersville, Prince Edward county. I hope that other hon. members, if they have met with this flouting of their purposes in being here, and the purposes of their representation in this chamber, will support me in this protest, because I am sure you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that this is a relevant and important point.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Can the hon. gentleman name another single member of this house who has had a similar experience? The hon. member is making general statements. Can he name a single member on either side of this house who is in that position? The hon. member's question is being studied, but will he answer my question? He is making a general statement and I should like to know whether he can name any single member in any corner of this house who is in the same position.
He doesn't get $27,000 a year to answer questions.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I can name a single person who is in that position, and that is myself, the representative of the people at Rednersville who have been wronged.

I said, "any other single person". If the hon. gentleman would listen, I said, "any single person other than himself". His case is being studied. Is there any other person in the house who has had a similar experience?

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words and make a suggestion which I think is quite relevant to the item

of "Publishing debates" because it has to do with the debates. Some time ago as the result of a committee study it was established that a member could send 16 Hansards in a complimentary way to his constituents. In talking generally with some other members in the past year or two I find I am not alone in not only having my complimentary list filled, but in having people ask me from time to time if they can get Hansard in this way. I know that some hon. members obtain an additional copy or two of Hansard and send them out under their own frank to individuals, just as though they were on a complimentary list.
I think it is a fairly general desire on the part of hon. members to have a larger number of complimentary Hansards available to them. I have heard the figure of 50 suggested and I have heard other figures suggested. Whatever figure is chosen, it would naturally have to be an arbitrary one; but I think some alteration should be made and there should be an increase in the number of complimentary Hansards available. As I have said, the number now is 16, which I think was established-I am guessing now, but it was perhaps 1948 or somewhere about that time; it may even have been before that period of time-and this number is not sufficient.
I leave this suggestion, Mr. Chairman, with the appropriate official of government that handles these things. Perhaps we could have a very short expression of opinion from hon. members of other parties as to whether they agree with the suggestion that the number of complimentary Hansards should be increased.

Before the item carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) that following the lack of proper organization of the business of the house, hon. members have had to sit at a time when they would normally have taken a recess. Consequently, a large proportion of the house staff has had to work under very trying conditions when they should normally have been enjoying a well-deserved rest.
As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, that is due mostly to the lack of organization shown by the government and I should like to point out especially to the President of the Privy Council who is engaged in a conversation with one of his colleagues at present, that he should look after the interests of the house staff. The latter had to work unusually hard due to the government's lack of foresight. I therefore submit that the staff should be compensated by means of additional holidays or by supplementary pay.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should let the remarks of the hon. member regarding questions on the order paper pass without my saying that I have had the utmost co-operation from the Clerk and assistant clerk of the house in connection with this matter. I do not think questions are put on the order paper to relate facts; I think they ask for information. I think the hon. member's problem is that he was making a statement which was not substantiated by the tabling of any items in this house. I want to say that I personally have had the utmost co-operation from the Clerk of the house.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I was making a statement substantiated by a letter from the former postmaster general in the month of September, 1963. I should like to ask the member who just took his seat how a person can ask a question without making statements relevant thereto. How can anyone form an interrogative sentence in the English language without a certain amount of assertion implied by the interrogative form of the sentence?

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say to the government that I will not press this particular matter now, but two hon. members have already made mention of the working conditions of some of the staff of the House of Commons. I will not elaborate on the matter but I should like to say that I know of no place where working conditions are as poor as the working conditions of many of the people who work in the House of Commons. I hope the commissioners of internal economy, with the Speaker, will review this situation so that we will not have to raise it again when the regular estimates come up. If some steps are not taken to deal with the general working conditions of the staff here we shall have to raise the matter at greater length when the general estimates are before the house.

Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS Dominion coal board-
140e. Payments in connection with the movements of coal under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, $3,914,600.
Mr. Chairman, this item calls for an expenditure of $3,941,600 and I think we should be entitled to an explanation from the minister as to what detail is involved here.

Mr. Chairman, I would join with my colleague from Skeena in asking the minister for some details of the tonnage of coal which is being transported under this
fMr. Martlneau.]

subsidy. At the same time he might give us a breakdown of the figures for coal shipments to Japan, which have been consistent with this subsidy. I would also urge the minister to consider a repeated request which I am sure he has received from coal operators asking that this subsidy, rather than being placed on an annual order in council basis as it is at the moment, be placed on a regular basis by the early introduction of legislation in this house which would provide, on a long term basis, fixed subsidies to the coal operators. This in turn would produce two results, one of which would be to let the operators themselves know just what assistance they can count on in the years to come. Also-and this is very important-it would assist importers of coal. I think particularly of the Japanese who have come to Canada on a number of occasions and asked the government to declare its policy over a number of years, so that they can make firm commitments over a period of three, five, or even ten years. I am sure that the minister, who has at heart the interests of the coal industry, will see that this legislation is introduced shortly, and we should like to have the figures and information requested both by the hon. member for Skeena and myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the business for tomorrow and for the days immediately ahead will be the same as announced last night. Tomorrow we shall try to complete,
I hope, the too short debate on the supplementary estimates. If there is some time left for other government business we will take second reading of the Canada pension plan bill. On the first available full day and on the second available full day, which might be Thursday and Friday, we will complete the budget debate. After that we will take up the resolution to set up a joint committee to study the Canada pension plan bill, following which we will carry on with the second reading of the Canada pension plan bill.
